before: This article asks whether that failure can arise without biased inference or an impaired learning rule. The target is deliberately narrow. The model concerns knowledge of two latent causes, baseline hazard and preventive efficacy. It does not attempt to reproduce the full phenomenology of compulsions; it isolates repeated preventive actions that alter a latent hazard. The following sections show that the missing comparison produces a structural identification problem.
after: This study asks what an accurate learner can infer when its own actions restrict the evidence it observes. The model isolates two latent quantities: baseline hazard and preventive efficacy. It explains why causal beliefs can remain wrong; it does not, by itself, explain why repetitive behaviour persists. The analysis concerns preventive actions that change a latent hazard, rather than the full range of compulsive symptoms.

before: Knowing whether an action controls an outcome requires variation in the action and comparison of the resulting outcomes. When failure is costly, the policy that minimises immediate risk can suppress exactly that variation. The same structure appears as a failure of persistent excitation in system identification, as self-confirming equilibrium in economics (Fudenberg & Levine, 1993), and as selective labels in machine learning (Lakkaraju et al., 2017). The clinical application motivates the model; the identification problem is more general. Fig 1 states the shift in one picture.

before: Knowledge is scored by the log posterior density at the true parameter, log P(q*,p* | D), not by entropy alone. Entropy rewards confidence, including the confidently wrong posterior produced by an untreated agent.
after: Accuracy is assessed using absolute error in posterior means, posterior standard deviations, and the log posterior density evaluated near the generating parameters. The implementation uses the first grid centre at or above each true coordinate, within one grid step (1/101). This log-density measure is a numerical approximation to the continuous log score, and its change is reported in natural-log units. It distinguishes concentrated error from useful learning, but depends on grid resolution. Entropy reduction is an additional diagnostic of uncertainty and does not by itself establish accuracy.

before: The residual dependence between q and p is therefore positive, and the ridge steepens with k: an agent that repeats more cannot tell a dangerous world it controls from a safe world it does not.
after: The likelihood ridge has a non-negative slope. At a given interior parameter pair, its slope increases with k: the same outcome rate can be explained by stronger prevention in a more hazardous world or weaker prevention in a safer world. This statement concerns the likelihood; posterior correlation also depends on the prior and observed outcomes.

before: Corollary 1 describes the likelihood. Posterior correlation also depends on how much information the outcomes contain. As k grows, λₖ → 0 and informative outcomes disappear, so posterior dependence can fall back towards zero. Fixed policies therefore create two distinct failures: at moderate k the learner estimates a combination it cannot decompose; at large k it learns little at all.
after: Corollary 1 describes likelihood geometry, not a universal ordering of posterior correlations. Posterior dependence also reflects the prior and the number of informative outcomes. At moderate k, the learner can estimate a combination it cannot decompose. At large k, harm becomes rare and even estimation of that combination can require many episodes.

before: so a policy with support on two distinct values of k point-identifies (q,p). In particular, at k=0 the likelihood (1) does not depend on p; response prevention alone identifies q and carries no information about p.
after: Thus two distinct action counts identify (q, p) when their exact outcome probabilities are known and (q, p) is interior. The result concerns identification, not guaranteed finite-sample recovery. At k = 0 the likelihood depends on q but not p. With an independent prior and only k = 0 observations, the marginal posterior for p remains unchanged. If earlier data have coupled q and p, observing q can instead update p indirectly.

before: For a policy π over repetition counts, information adds as I_π = nΣₖ π(k) Iₖ. The support of π, not its mean, determines rank. In control-theoretic terms, a fixed policy fails to persistently excite the system: it can reduce immediate risk while remaining uninformative about the system's causal parameters (Bellman & Åström, 1970).
after: For an externally assigned distribution π over action counts, the expected information after n episodes is Iπ = n Σₖ π(k) Iₖ. Positive allocation to two distinct counts makes this matrix full rank at interior parameters. Consistent estimation also requires adequate sampling at informative counts. Adaptive policies are analysed conditional on the recorded action history. This is a simple instance of the design dependence of structural identifiability (Bellman & Åström, 1970).

before: The signature of the trap is the contrast between what is learned and what is not. The repetitive agent gains 4.80 nats about the observable composite λₖ and -0.58 nats about p (the learning summary). The same contrast in scale-free terms is starker still: relative to its prior, the agent's posterior standard deviation for the observable λ₆ shrinks by a factor of 151, while its uncertainty about p does not shrink at all - it grows, by a factor of 1/0.63, as the data push it off a prior that was narrow and wrong onto a ridge that is broad. It can predict what will happen to it with great precision while becoming less sure why. The diversified agent shows the opposite pattern: 17× on the observable and 2.73× on the parameter. (The ratios accompany the entropies because the entropy of λₖ is computed on a fixed [0,1] bin grid and saturates when λₖ becomes very small, so the nats figure is a lower bound on the information gained.) The repetitive agent's final posterior lies along the analytic ridge (Fig 3C); the diversified agent's sits at the intersection of the ridges belonging to the different k it used (Fig 3D).
after: The fixed-policy learner reduces the posterior standard deviation of the observable composite λₖ by a factor of 151, while its efficacy uncertainty increases by a factor of about 1.59. Its outcome predictions therefore improve without comparable accuracy about their causes. The variable-policy learner instead recovers both parameters. The final posteriors in Fig. 3c,d show one representative agent per condition. Realized entropy reductions can be negative and are not the same quantity as the non-negative expected information gain used in the policy. For very small λₖ, the histogram-based entropy also has limited resolution.

before: Response prevention is not a probe of efficacy. With no repetitive history to contrast against, response prevention moves the agent's efficacy belief by 0.000 - exactly nothing, as Proposition 2 requires - while the same intervention applied after a repetitive block moves it by 0.57. Earlier repetitive episodes pin down the composite λₖ, response-prevention episodes pin down q, and the two together determine p. Response prevention works as the second half of a contrast and is inert as the first half.
after: Response prevention does not directly identify efficacy. The independent severe-doubt prior followed only by k = 0 episodes leaves the efficacy mean unchanged. In the simulated comparison, the no-repetition reference receives 400 initial and 600 intervention episodes at k = 0; only its subsequent follow-up permits free choice. By contrast, k = 0 after a block containing preventive actions changes the efficacy posterior because earlier outcomes have coupled q and p. Response prevention provides an informative second condition, but its usefulness also depends on what was observed before it.

before: Probe timing separates state and causal information. A state probe performed after the preventive action removes 0.021 nats of current-state uncertainty while adding only 2.4 nats of structural knowledge, against 7.1 for the diversified policy (Fig 4C). Moving the same probe before the action yields 8.5 nats. Its cost and accuracy are unchanged; only its position in the causal sequence differs. A post-action observation can establish that the current outcome is safe without showing whether the action produced that safety.
after: Probe timing separates immediate uncertainty from parameter learning. A post-action probe reduces mean state entropy at commitment by 0.021 nats and changes the approximate log-density score by 2.4 over the intervention block; the variable-k condition changes the score by 7.1 (Fig. 4c). The post-action probe itself adds no parameter information conditional on the noiseless terminal outcome; its score change comes from the terminal outcomes and the realized action history. Moving the probe before action yields a score change of 8.5. The sensitivity and specificity remain 0.80; the joint likelihood accounts for the shared state within each episode.

before: The trap has no fixed behavioural direction. By the end of the pre-treatment block every agent has settled at k ≈ 1.87 with E[p| D] = 0.28 - still far below the true 0.80 - and, more strikingly, E[q| D] = 0.10 against a true baseline hazard of 0.30, a value its own posterior places 5.9 standard deviations away. The trapped agent has resolved its non-identifiability in the wrong direction: it has concluded that the world is safe rather than that its actions work. Every condition that supplies a genuine probe of q corrects this (E[q| D] = 0.27 under diversified exposure, against 0.07 if untreated) and consequently raises the follow-up repetition rate, to 2.98 against 1.97 for the untreated agent, with pure response prevention highest at 2.98.
after: Belief correction does not imply fewer actions in this model. The seven arms with a preventive baseline share the same protocol and prior but use different random seeds. Across those arms, the baseline efficacy mean is about 0.31 and the hazard mean about 0.07, compared with true values 0.80 and 0.30. The learner therefore underestimates hazard as well as efficacy. Correcting hazard under variable action counts increases the follow-up hazard estimate to 0.27, compared with 0.075 under continued free choice. The highest follow-up action count among the diversified conditions is 2.98, compared with 1.97 in the untreated reference.

before: A direct causal test should assign the action schedule rather than infer its effect from naturally varying behaviour. Participants would complete a computerized latent-hazard task in one of four between-participant conditions: k=3 on every trial, equal mixtures of k∈{2,4}, equal mixtures of k∈{1,5}, or a uniform schedule over k∈{0,,6} (Fig 5A). Every schedule has E[k]=3, so the number of actions and their total cost are matched. The {1,5} and uniform schedules also have the same raw variance, Var(k)=4, but distribute observations differently. Their contrast separates the amount of variation from the information carried by its support.
after: A human test would assign action schedules rather than infer their effect from naturally varying behaviour. Four between-participant conditions would use k = 3, equal mixtures of {2, 4}, equal mixtures of {1, 5}, or uniform counts from 0 to 6 (Fig. 5a). All have mean action count 3; {1, 5} and uniform 0–6 also have variance 4. Randomly ordered, balanced 14-trial blocks would give every condition exactly 42 actions per block. This matches action burden and cost, while distinguishing raw variance from the informational support of a schedule. The existing simulations match these quantities in expectation, using independent draws rather than exactly balanced blocks.

before: Participants would observe only the terminal binary outcome. before: The simulation yields three ordered predictions. First, the fixed schedule should produce the least precise and least accurate efficacy estimates. Second, varying the action count should improve learning even when mean exposure is unchanged. Third, the uniform schedule should outperform {1,5} despite equal means and variances, because it samples more informative outcomes (Fig 5B,C). Across conditions, expected Fisher information or expected information gain should predict efficacy accuracy better than raw Var(k).
after: The simulations motivate two primary contrasts. Informative variation should improve final efficacy estimates relative to fixed k = 3. Uniform 0–6 should also outperform {1, 5} despite their equal means and variances (Fig. 5b,c). Expected Fisher information or information gain should be evaluated against simpler predictors such as variance and realized event counts. Matching mean action count does not match expected harm: q E[(1 − p)^k] differs across schedules. Event frequency is part of the proposed mechanism, so these comparisons alone cannot establish an effect independent of experienced harm. Models should be fitted to the actual action and outcome history; complementary designs would be needed to isolate an event-frequency explanation.

before: The true values of (q,p), number of trials, and sample size should be fixed only after simulation-based parameter-recovery and power analyses. In particular, a regime that makes harm almost absent under k=3 would provide too few events for a practical human test even though it illustrates the theorem. The account would be challenged if an adequately powered and recoverable experiment found no advantage of informative variation over the fixed schedule, or if schedules with equal raw variance produced indistinguishable learning despite different expected information.
after: The generating parameters, trial count and participant sample size should be chosen after parameter-recovery, model-comparison and power simulations for a feasible laboratory task. The final trial count should permit complete balanced blocks. The proposed experiment has not been preregistered or conducted. A recoverable and adequately powered design showing no benefit of informative variation would challenge the account; an underpowered null result or an unrecoverable parameter regime would not provide that test.

before: The hazard model is a deliberate reduction. The agent commits to k before the episode rather than choosing action by action. The environment is stationary except in the path-dependence analysis, and change is handled by exponential forgetting rather than a change-point model. Harm is observed without noise; adding observation noise would not restore identification and would generally reduce information. The intervention simulations isolate action-count variation, whereas real exposure and response prevention changes several processes at once.
after: The hazard model deliberately restricts the available evidence. Each episode begins with an independent latent hazard, the agent commits to k in advance, successful prevention removes the hazard for the rest of that episode, and the terminal outcome reveals the final state without noise. Action-dependent cues or state observations can change identification; the theorem applies to terminal-outcome-only, fixed-count designs. The non-stationary supplement uses power-discounted posteriors rather than exact Bayesian inference in a change-point model. Its results illustrate delayed recalibration under that approximation. The analytic theorem concerns continuous parameters. A finite grid does not represent an entire likelihood ridge exactly and can alter asymptotic behaviour. Grid-refinement tests check selected posterior means, not every reported effect or extreme prior setting.

before: What organises the whole diagram is the realised repetition count, and it does so in the shape of a U (Fig S1D). before: The information-seeking weight is the escape axis, and what it changes is instructive. Among the most doubtful third of agents, residual error falls from 0.26 at τ=0 to 0.13 at τ=300, and the efficacy belief moves from 0.54 to 0.67 against a true 0.80. What it changes to achieve this is worth being precise about, because it is not what one might guess. The agent does not act much less (2.17 repetitions against 2.30), and it does not visibly vary more (variance of the action count 0.118 against 0.123). What rises is the harm it actually experiences, from 1.0% of episodes to 1.7%. The escape is a shift towards repetition counts at which outcomes still happen, which is the same lesson the policy comparison in Fig 2B teaches: a "compulsive but jittered" policy on k ∈ {5,6,7} is formally non-singular and practically useless. Variation buys nothing where nothing ever occurs.

before: Ramping the objective hazard up and back down (Fig S2) produces history dependence in every arm. A loop alone is not diagnostic because any belief-updating agent lags a moving world; indeed, loop areas do not separate the arms (0.36 for the locked design against 0.38 for an agent with a standing 25% response-prevention quota). What does separate them is calibration, and it does so asymmetrically. On the rising limb every arm tracks the hazard about equally well (|E[q| D]-q| = 0.103 up, against 0.100 up). On the falling limb the locked design comes apart: 0.172 against 0.115 for the quota agent and 0.108 for an agent with a pre-action state probe. The trap is specifically a failure to notice that the world has become safer, which is what the theory predicts: the evidence that would carry that news is the evidence a repetitive policy suppresses.

before: The locked agent's terminal beliefs show the ridge directly. It ends convinced both that its actions are highly effective (E[p| D] = 0.80) and that the world remains dangerous (0.323) - a pair that reproduces the harm rate it observes (namely zero) exactly as well as the truth does. Every arm that supplies a contrast converges instead on the correct low hazard. The result concerns delayed belief recalibration under constrained policies. It does not show that the model endogenously generates chronic compulsive behaviour.
after: Under the concentrated softmax condition, terminal beliefs retain both elevated efficacy and a positive hazard estimate despite the absence of observed harm. Such beliefs can assign a low probability to harm; zero observed events do not imply zero generating probability or exact equality with the true likelihood. The comparison concerns delayed recalibration under constrained evidence and posterior discounting, not endogenous chronic compulsive behaviour.
